title: null and nullable values
hook: `null` is a reference value. `int` cannot be `null` unless you wrap it as `int?` (`Nullable<int>`). Nullable reference types are a later compiler overlay (module 07), not this story.

sections.heading: int? versus reference null
sections.prose: Reference types can hold `null` — no object. Value types cannot, until you use `T?` which is `Nullable<T>`: a struct with `HasValue` and `Value`. `int? ttl = cache.GetTtl();` models a missing Redis TTL. Lifted operators let you write `ttl + 1` (result is `int?`). Use `ttl ?? 30`, `ttl.GetValueOrDefault()`, or `if (ttl is int seconds)`. Do not confuse this with NRT: `string?` in a nullable-enabled project is still a reference `string` plus an annotation; `int?` is a different runtime type. Module 07 covers `#nullable`, annotations, and `!`. Here: missing values for structs need `Nullable<T>`; missing objects are `null`.

snippets.label: Nullable value vs reference
snippets.explanation: int? is a value-type wrapper. string? is still a reference. Operators ?? and ?. apply to both in the ways you saw in module 02.

interviewTakeaways: `T?` on a value type is `Nullable<T>` — a different struct.
`T?` on a reference type (NRT) is the same CLR type with annotations — module 07.
commonPitfalls: Using `== null` on a `Nullable<T>` when `is null` / pattern is clearer, but both work.
Storing Redis misses as `0` instead of `int?` and colliding with a real zero TTL.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS has both `null` and `undefined`. C# locals cannot be unread; optional values are `null` or `T?`. No separate undefined.
`number | null` is a union erased at run time. `int?` is a real Nullable wrapper. `string | null` is closer to annotated `string?`.
